title: The Anglepoise lamp's springs
hook: A desk lamp that stays where you point it came from a car suspension engineer.
peek: George Carwardine spent his working life on vehicle suspension. In the early 1930s he used what he knew about springs to build a jointed arm that holds any position, and the Anglepoise desk lamp was born.
lede: George Carwardine was an English engineer who specialised in car suspension. He was not trying to make a lamp. He wanted an arm that could be moved freely yet stay put wherever it was left, like a human limb held by its muscles. His answer, patented in 1932, balanced each joint with springs, and the first thing he fitted to the end was a light.

bullets.text: The springs are arranged so their pull matches the weight of the arm at every angle. Nothing has to be clamped or tightened, so the lamp can be pushed into a new position with one finger and stays there.
Carwardine licensed the design to Herbert Terry and Sons, a spring maker in Redditch, which already supplied his springs. In 1935 Terry's launched the three-spring Anglepoise Model 1227 for the home.

In 1937 the Norwegian Jac Jacobsen licensed Carwardine's design and adapted it as the Luxo L-1. That lamp is the one Pixar animated in its 1986 short Luxo Jr., which is why a hopping lamp opens Pixar films.
The springs were new ones designed for the lamp, not parts taken from a car. What came from cars was Carwardine's know-how about how springs carry a load.
